label: Cheirality: Which Side of the Camera
notes: Open by stressing that reprojection alone cannot tell front from back. Cheirality is the orientation information a bare projective reconstruction discards. Across these printed pages we make positive depth, quasi-affine structure, the cheiral inequalities, and the essential-matrix four-fold ambiguity into executable sign tests, not vague intuitions.

label: Signed Projective Depth
notes: Define depth as a signed quantity built from three pieces: the third row of the projection, the determinant sign of the left block, and the homogeneous representative. Emphasize that the raw third coordinate of P X is not enough; without the determinant and scale factors the sign is meaningless and not invariant.

label: Front or Back Is Sign of w
notes: Walk through the two-panel notebook figure. Every synthetic point sits in front of the first camera, yet far points fall behind the third camera once its principal plane shifts. The lesson: front versus back is purely the sign of the depth scalar w, evaluated camera by camera.

label: Projective Ambiguity Loses Cheirality
notes: Explain that an arbitrary projective transform can flip a point across the plane at infinity, swapping its depth sign while preserving all image measurements. This is why reconstruction from correspondences alone leaves orientation undetermined and motivates restricting the transformation to those that respect cheirality.

label: Quasi-Affine Reconstruction
notes: Position quasi-affine between projective and affine. It does not recover the plane at infinity exactly, but it keeps that plane from slicing through the visible point set. Stress the convex-hull picture: enforcing cheirality fixes which side of infinity the scene lies on without metric data.

label: One Sign on the Convex Hull
notes: Use the four-panel notebook result. A quasi-affine map keeps the last homogeneous coordinate one sign across the whole convex hull; a non-quasi-affine map lets that denominator change sign, so the line sent to infinity cuts the finite hull. The denominator sign is the computable test.

label: The Cheiral Inequalities
notes: State the inequalities precisely after representative signs are fixed: points must satisfy X transpose v positive, centres must satisfy delta times C transpose v positive. The vector v encodes the candidate plane at infinity and delta is the orientation sign of the transform. These are linear half-space constraints.

label: Feasibility as a Linear Program
notes: Show how the strict inequalities become a margin-maximizing linear program: maximize d subject to each a transpose v at least d. A positive optimal margin is a numerical certificate that the side assignment is consistent. Walk the audience from geometry to the linprog formulation in the notebook.

label: Separating Plane and Orientation
notes: Connect the two delta cells to geometry. When a plane separates all camera centres from all visible points, both orientations stay feasible and an opposite-orientation realization survives. Interleave a camera among the points and the delta equals minus one cell vanishes, removing that ambiguity.

label: The Essential-Matrix Four-Fold Ambiguity
notes: Recall that decomposing E gives rotation from two choices and translation up to sign, yielding four candidate camera pairs. Only one places a reconstructed point in front of both cameras. Frame the cheirality test as the standard tiebreaker that selects the physically correct pose.

label: Cheirality Test Picks the Pose
notes: Walk the four-panel schematic. Three candidates put the point behind at least one camera, drawn as a back-side ray; the fourth puts it in front of both. Triangulate one correspondence, check both depth signs, and keep the configuration with two positive depths.

label: Third View, Depth Order, Recap
notes: Close with downstream consequences. A known visible anchor and the sign of w1 times w3 classify visibility in a third view; inverse depth orders points on a shared ray once orientation is fixed. Recap: carry the sign information alongside the projective equations before trusting the scene.
